You can have all the rules in the world--and in fact, U.S. Soccer imposes clear-cut guidelines that tell referees what to do in just such situations: "Allow goals and penalty kicks, as appropriate, even if the necessary mark is inadvertently made by an attacking player's hand/arm." The authors of the publication, U.S. Soccer calls it the Procedural Guide for Referees, and Explain Expanded League Assessment Program, say that "referees need to be very careful when they are distinguishing between unintentional handball and deliberate movements of the hand/arm to handle the ball."

But sometimes the rules get murky.

In baseball umpires have replay; when a ball is hit so far it can't be tracked precisely, umpires call for video replays and render a decision on the reliability of the original call. Soccer has no replay. It has game tape, which comes in useful for various kinds of statistics (saves, long passes, corner kicks). But referees don't see the tape. So all the historical precedence and the lessons in the referee guide aren't as useful as game tape would be. It's kind of like MLB's historical data, all those box scores and scorecards, but without grainy video to go back to. In this century that doesn't always work.

Ever since the willful misconduct card was introduced for English professional soccer in the 2004–05 season, successful appeals are capped at 1,500 pounds (about $3,300). This means that the appeals that make sense are the ones worth less than 1,500 pounds. Why tie up your team for a week and a half arguing a case in which you can expect to save your company no more than one full salary?

But what about the huge awards, the thousands of pounds? Maybe those represent games that should have been given to the other team. Maybe the insider Web site Soccer Outlook, which is the mother lode for game-fixing evidence (a jury recently decided that it couldn't serve investigators with a subpoena), works too quickly, leaking out the emails between insiders in too short order. Maybe the process is fairer than it looks. At least it's more transparent than the NFL appeals process, in which each side — the league and the players — has its own paid arbitrator. Suppose, for example, that the NFL has its own biometrician who's a statistician-ex–football player, according to a recent story in Deadspin, who wears an eye patch and has a signature procedure of making players take field sobriety tests in the scripted moments before he enters the room and sits down in his trademark chair. You might conclude that's just a little nuts, and then you might want to ask why they have such a guy in the first place.

The NFL's comparisons to other sports divisions — whether it's a league of owners or a league of teams — must come with the usual caveats when discussing sports economics: Its gross revenue compares to Europe's Premier League, and its franchise values compare to Major League Baseball. But in terms of its operational arrangements, it is more like the NCAA. To create the sort of confrontation that animates, for example, a Yankees–Red Sox game, the NFL players have had to form their own b.s. wing of labor relations so as to motivate their employer to open talks. When baseball locked out its players for months during the 1994 season, they decertified the MLBPA with five minutes of leeway left in mediation, so that the key players would be leverage in avoiding a salary cap. Now the NFLPA is following the same playbook, and the NFL has launched decertification proceedings against the players. It's like there's nobody calling the timeout.

Mike reached the edge of the field. In his black-and-gold striped shirt and black flag-belt, with his dad haircut and blank unsmiling face, he'd been a powerful, slightly intimidating figure. Now he stopped.

Deja vu

Mike was a visiting NCAA and FIFA official and the national coach for U.S. Soccer. He'd spent hundreds of games with officials over the years and had talked to them about every angle of soccer--training, financial struggles, complicated rules, sneaky managers. He'd told them for years that youth coaches would be the most important babysitters for the game. Mike played soccer to a high level all through high school, but it was six weeks of intense summer leagues starting at 8 a.m. every day and running till long after dark that fired his passion. The fun killed him, the working-togetherness killed him, and as long as he was in the game, its future depended on kids making a similar kind of addictive commitment.

State youth referees are kind of non-people in Arizona. The U.S. Soccer youth coaching curriculum offers nothing about the skill set of refereeing, so there is no education, no standard that allows referees to be ranked, no route to advancement. Azsudo, Arizona's soccer governing body, offers no referee source. Soccer Canada certifies its volunteers, but in the United States the league officials and state federations certify and oversee them, and they have staffs one hundredth the size they were five years ago. Capital wisdom has it that the referee crisis will cure itself. The Central California League (better known as the CCL) is an unusual beast in the world of youth soccer.

The CCL is a statewide league that organizes games at the regional level. In Tulare County, its affiliate is the Sunday Valley Soccer League (SVSL), which is made up of thirteen clubs spread throughout a largely rural area that every person who lives there refers to as "the Valley" because the Tulare County section of unincorporated Kings County (the Riverdale-Amsden area) is also known as Valley, and all of the little villages just outside the Valley, like Lindsay and Woodlake and Orosi, are also known as "the Valley," and all of the play in the CCL/SVSL takes place on that land. The only other town in the county is the city of Tulare, which is part of the San Joaquin Valley but isn't the Valley, either.

Also, it should be noted that while it is the administrative seat of the county, the city of Tulare is little more than a glorified truck stop resting on the side of Highway 99 some fifteen-odd miles from the Valley's big towns.

So the CCL/SVSL is massive: It includes cities and towns scattered across more than five thousand square miles, so many hours away from anybody else that you probably talk to them less often than you speak to people from Belgium. The CCL was also the first statewide league to not include batches of teams from different schools wanting to play just one another. Nor was it just an extension of a recreational program. Here's what Mike Delgado saw from his angle:

When the assistant referee tells me where to stand, I take the inside spot, about four yards from, and a little behind, the top of the penalty box, and I look at the final approach. I call everything with my back to the goal, closed books.

That one came from the right side. It was a yellow jersey—these kids' schedules are tight, and they play everywhere, so they're always sharing jerseys—and it was a kick, not a dribble; kicks are sharps, cuts are softs. The ball was played early, just after it hit the chest of the defensive line, and came across me at waist high.

The striker started outside the box, and as the ball came across he cut inside and passed me, slow and heavy. I don't see completions; I watch closers. When he moved into my partition I stood up straighter and planted my feet and watched him watch the ball. I had no doubt it was going on the ground between us, that he would finish it. So I backed up and came down to the play.

He planted his nonstriking foot next to mine and turned and moved his hips and brought his striking foot across, low and tight, the same side as the pass. It came off the instep and had some curl, but not much; it creaved up the middle of the box and went in.

So it was a left-footed shot from perhaps 35 yards out, hit on the far side of my body. I saw the ball all the way, from the moment it left his foot.

Mike and the other ref were the only ones who knew which way he'd ruled plays like that all his eight years, and you couldn't look that stuff up. What mattered was that whoever got the whistle would know what he would have called, and the players would believe it too. Neither coach had said a word to question or challenge him. The assistant had been working with him off to the side for six weeks. "I've seen you call it both ways," the assistant said.

It happened to him more often than not, this feeling that he was just barely keeping up with the game, and what he knew and what he was seeing and what he was supposed to do. He'd come into the parents' room at halftime at the scorekeeper's table and sit and watch the other games on the big screen, and he'd feel that way then too. Maybe everybody felt like that. He took the whistle out of his mouth and blew to bring the players back in.

The penalty kick rules were simple. The defense had to stand on the goal line, outside the goal, the goalkeeper standing in front of the goal, both hands on the ball. The offense, from twenty yards away, got one on the shot itself, no tricks, no fakes. Once the shot was taken, even if the goalkeeper had moved early, the kick had to be allowed to go in.

'A Call From the Heart'

A referee is supposed to control a match, calm and steady, referee. But when Mike stepped off the field, he was shaking like he'd played in it.

It isn't easy calling fouls against kids. The kids are fast and small and bored, and unless they're winning they get frustrated and run around like madmen. Roving groups of players look for any pretext for contact, testing each other and the referee, and they grow wilder and more aggressive in stoppage time, when players are tired and tempers short. You see the same things at the adult level--only faster.

Mike studied video of professional matches for hints of how to referee college games, to train his eyes. Some of the best American refs call more fouls against their own players than the opponents', on the theory that own calls establish credibility. Officiating American-style rugby is like refereeing an episode of COPS.

The rules are complex, but the referee is required first to decide whether the ball was deliberately kicked, punched or thrown to a player by his own teammate, the last being an offense called "passing to the goalkeeper with the hand" whose only penalty is the retake of the kick.

If the action is legal, which was the case here, the game cannot simply end, because the goalkeeping rules exist precisely so that inadvertent or even deliberate touches with the hand do not necessarily end the game (unlike, for example, a handball by a field player). The referee must therefore allow the opponents one quick, "goalkeeping" free kick, where the passer may use his hands, taken from the relevant spot (where the ball was handled), in Mike's case the spot where the ball first hit the ground.

The Hawks players — including Luis — formed a defensive line. The Ranger players spread out and took aim. It looked like they were going to walk it in and win.

The ball came back to the quarterback. His first kick sailed over the wall of defenders, where Mike was standing with the rest of the Hawks.

Because the shot was a free kick and did not need to wait for the ball to be played dead, the rules permit the goalkeeper to move once the kick has been taken. Luis, who had held a very deep position, ran in as the Ranger's kick came down and batted it away, the ball now staying live and remaining the property of his team.

As Luis chased down the ball, he drifted just outside the box, but by the time he got to it three Rangers backs had rushed in to play it. There was a tackle, and Angel drive, a short distance later bumbled the ball into his own net.

The assistant referee said nothing. There was no goal-line technology; hypothetically it was possible that the ball had not actually crossed the line and his flag should have stayed down. More unlikely, the ball had actually crossed the line and he would have been required by the rules to raise his flag even if he was not 100 percent certain.

Mike blew his whistle. The game was over. The Hawks were going to state. If he was wrong and had cost them that chance, Mike would never forgive himself.

He blew again, and they had penalty kicks.

The crossbar was at regulation height and the goal size was regulation, but the second-string goalkeepers had been practicing at the higher school goals, so they kicked to the top.

Luis had gone back to the sideline and thrown himself on the grass, sobbing. Mike went to him, knelt and put his arms around him. A Mariners coach had come up to say the kid was going to be okay. Mike and his wife would later console an opponent's mother, whose son had just missed the winning kick.

Mike was furious with himself for the rest of the night. He'd made up his mind on the hand while the ball was still in the air, but that wasn't how it was supposed to work. The hand is cunning. It disguises itself. You don't jump to conclusions.

Another referee such a call might have gone the other way and properly given the goal. That’s what people said. And maybe Mike heard them.

But more than twenty years after he looked at the ball and then the hand and saw what he saw, Mike still remembered something. During his years in Tulare County he usually did about fifteen or twenty games a year and sometimes kept track of players. The week before, Luis had been playing for the West Coast All-Stars against an All-Stars team from Stockton, and Luis had scored the only goal of the game. Mike was the referee. He had been expecting the pass and the shot the whole morning, and when it happened and the goal was scored he couldn't help himself. He ran several yards into the goal and held Luis up while he celebrated.

“I'll never forget that,” Mike said. “I knew it was going to happen. The whole time I'm running up, I'm thinking, I want to be the ref who lets him score. But I'm still the ref. I can't be the coach, right?”

“The hardest thing you have to do as a referee is deny your kid something. But if you don't deny him at home under the same rules, then you deny everyone else. So I had to make the call. I had to. I had to.”

A rule that every youth soccer coach in the country knows is this: Any time the ball is not purposely kicked, it is played by whatever part of the player's body it touches. Hands are not the most stationary part of a body; a hand that touches the ball and does not convey it is exactly the same as a foot that touches the ball and does not convey it.

On a day when everything was going wrong for the Rangers, Mike Delgado's whistle meant this: sudden death, best-of-three shootout. Every miss meant one player on the other team could shoot unopposed.

It seemed nearly unfair that the Rangers had given the game to the Hawks with their own hands and feet, but no—Mike Delgado had called it correctly. Out of all the possible moments for this game to come down to the judgment of a referee, it was, without question, the best one.

The first shot ricocheted off the crossbar. The second missed, sailing wide. Then the Hawks came back on offense, and on their third possession, the keeper played a short ball back to his line, missed a pass, and played it right to Luis, who had read the play all along. Luis tapped it home, and his team rushed him.

By the time the Hawks lifted Luis on their shoulders, Mike was crying. He never saw what happened after that.

It doesn't bother him, the hypothetical question. To this day, he won't say what he would have done if his son hadn't scored. He doesn't want to know. "I don't lie about that," he says. It's easier to live with the idea that he let his son decide, and that yes, other kids think he's soft on his own kids. He's willing to deal with that. And when a question finally did force him to make the call, two years later, it turned out the same way. But that's a different story.

Mike still refereed that same older age group, through the summer and on into this fall. But by October both his kids were on his weekend schedule. He would watch other parents chase their kids and try to influence the referees. Every time he saw it, he thought, That's what I have to avoid becoming. Coaches can coach. He can't. The job is to make sure his kids play against better teams, not softer ones.

His phone still rings occasionally with lineup changes. He remembers the feeling each time: the world briefly shifting to make room for him.

Patrick Hruby lives in Tucson, Arizona.

Matt Myers, the Coach of the Rangers, called it "heartbreaking" that Mike had made a call in his own son's favor, and he wrote an email to the tournament director saying that "everyone here at J&D [Sports] is very disappointed in the poor sportsmanship" displayed by "two dads."

Mike disagreed with that. "I've made these calls before," he told me. It had cost his own son a goal once or twice—why would he break the rule now? Parents can be louder about these things when their child is playing in the final, he said, but he'd referee another game the next weekend and it wouldn't matter to them anymore.

For two weeks after the game, Luis kept taking his equipment out of the closet and pretending to practice. Then the family drove to Phoenix, and he joined a travel team at his new school.

He hadn't intended to take that hand-ball, Mike said. It was just that they'd practiced that play a dozen times, and Luis knew it was coming and he wanted to help his team win. "He made a mistake," Mike said, "and he has to live with that." What Mike couldn't say was that he knew the feeling. When he told me the story, eight months later, his voice started to shake when he described the whistle he blew. Being a parent and being a referee had always been completely separate things for him, he said. On that day they'd collided.

What else could he have done?

Mike held the jersey and watched his son walk to the parking lot with his team.

He'd blown a lot of calls, he knew. He'd been too quick to point a red card. The hand ball had been borderline. But that was the call everybody expected him to make, and that was how it had to be. He had made the right call on the goalkeeper, though. Grabbing a bouncing ball with your hands was never, ever all right.

He kept the jersey for a week and then gave it to Luis. And when he and his family moved to Arizona, he found another youth-soccer league and signed up to referee again. Soccer has no offense quite like the hand ball, unless it's a deliberate hand ball, which this was not. Mike checked with the other referee to be sure he'd seen the same thing. He did. Then he gave his younger son a kick ball in the back and sent him to his team's end for the restart.

The coaches and most of the players accepted the result. A few players glared at Luis when they jogging off, but not one of them shouted at him. Luis had broken a rule, clearly and for the final time, but not a sacred one. Nobody betrayed anybody on purpose.

Afterward Mike felt terrible for a moment, knowing he'd just cost his son a trip to the state tournament, knowing that every victory his son won from here on would be against different teams - his old friends and rivals were headed east while his family headed west. Then it occurred to him that if he had called it the other way, the memory would never have left him. He might second-guess that call every day for the rest of his life. If there's one thing parents who referee their kids' games learn, it's that the right call is the only call that lets you go to sleep at night.

The Rangers coach couldn't believe it. Nobody had seen that. His tone turned bitingly sarcastic as he demanded to know which law said a handball had to be called from 18 yards away. Mike said nothing. He held up two fingers, then three while he counted down the time-wastinganskids.

The kick came. It curved inside the far post and ricocheted into the net. The scoreboard beside the field flashed 2–1. Mike blew a final whistle, cupped his hands around his mouth and yelled, "Great game!" and then jogged off the field before the congratulations started coming his way.

In the parking lot, nobody who worked for the city was willing to see him. That was the rule. It didn't matter that the assistant referee had told the park supervisor he hadn't had a clear view. Mike got in the car and started the engine. His wife asked him how it went.

"I saved it for you," he said.

She pulled a photo album from the backseat and opened to a page filled with pictures of Luis. On the back of one of them, he'd written, "To my future State Champion." Luis had been sure the photo was of him in the trophy ceremony, but Mike promised he'd fill it in later.

Mike slid the album back into the seat, locked the doors and sat for a moment. The dashboard clock read 7:28. In eight minutes they'd be late for dinner; in ten, they would be on the highway out of Tulare County for the last time, driving east toward the dark mountains and then the flat gray desert and then Phoenix.

Mike took a deep breath and looked at his son in the backseat, already talking about playing for the high school team next year. In the rearview mirror, Mike watched the reflection shrink until it was gone, the stands and the goalie net and the field where he had seen every one of Luis's games fade into the night behind them.

The same kids who scorned officials when they disagreed with calls now wanted him to hand them the championship. He cued the video monitor by the grandstand and watched the replay, the ball thumping into Luis's palm, probably hard enough to hurt. It was an obvious, textbook handball.

Mike waited until the video ended and then pointed to the spot again. "Indirect free kick to the defense," he said. There was no celebration; the Rangers had already trudged toward the midfield circle as if they knew. They barely looked at Mike until they left the field to an obligatory handshake line, and even then nobody made eye contact with the official.

Mike blew the final whistle and jogged off the pitch as the teams went to the penalty-spot positions for kicks, the Hawks already preparing to celebrate. A few parents and coaches thanked him, and a couple of kids said sorry for what had happened, and Mike thanked them back, although he suspected they were feeling sorry for the wrong thing.

He found Luis hugging Sam, his best friend, whose save had sent the game to overtime. Luis looked at his father and said, "Sorry, Dad," and Mike nodded and tried not to smile and tried not to cry.

They went to the parking lot for the postgame pizza party—Losers Buy—where for the next hour nobody mentioned what had happened. "Sorry, Lu," a Rangers defender finally said, and Luis just shrugged and nodded.

The Rules

• In soccer, a handball is punished with either a direct free kick (if the hand/arm is deliberately moved to the ball) or an indirect free kick (if the hand/arm touches the ball accidentally).

• A deliberate handball is clearly a foul; the dilemma arises when the handball is an accident.

• Young players rarely make a deliberate attempt to stop the ball with their hands unless they are desperate (or being foolish). That implies that almost every handball by a non-goalie is an accidental one.

Mike raised his arm and showed the first red card of his career. Then he blew his whistle again and pointed to the penalty spot. If Mike had called the hand ball and just awarded a kick, it might've been the end of the game. There might've been shouting but not the kind of shouting there was now. One of the Rangers mothers started shouting before the kick went in. "That's ridiculous!" she called. "You can't just—!"

Mike blew his whistle a third time and held the card he'd just shown up to make sure the players could see it. Then he put his hands to his mouth and shouted, "That's exactly what I just did!"

You couldn't really argue with that, and after the game only a few people did, briefly. The rest of the time they talked about the penalty kick Luis buried, the save the Rangers' keeper made on the first kick, the miss on the second. The Hawks lost, two kicks to four.

Mike shook the Rangers' coach's hand after the game and apologized. "I don't know," he said. "Sometimes you have to make a call, and you know it's not popular. I just thought it was the only call I could make."

And that was true. He knew it wasn't popular. Someone had already called him a coward on the Internet. But he also knew what the right call was, and he also knew that sometimes the right call needs a referee willing to make it.

The law is the law

Every dad on the Rangers bench was shouting at him now. Mike was looking at his father-in-law, who was the other assistant. His phone would buzz after the game with all the reasons he was wrong. He didn't care. The handball law is the law. Nobody in the country works harder at youth sports than California kids—players and referees alike. You have to hold them to those laws, because that's the only way they learn them.

Or they have a chance to learn them, anyway. That's why Mike does it. That's why he's spending his last weekend here in the heat with these dusty fields and volunteer coaches and 10-year-olds crying when their parents pick them up and they don't make a team.

If you start making exceptions, you're not teaching the kids anything. You're not preparing them for the next level. And it's cheating, and you know it. If you can't be fair, you have no right to be out there.

"That's a terrible call," one of the Rangers coaches told him when it was over. Hawks 3, Rangers 1.

"Sorry," Mike answered. "It's not my call."

Rangers coach John Mendoza disagreed, and he made sure to tell Mike that his call had been wrong. "That's ok," Mike said. "I'm supposed to be the bad guy."

The families of the other teams waited by their cars, and Mike and Luis hugged at midfield. Then the two teams lined up for the handshakes they teach kids to do at the end of matches, and Mike stood with his referee crew and watched them. They had handled it well. Shaking hands after a tough loss is hard when you're 14. But they had done it.

Mike's wife was in the SUV with the three kids, getting the car seats ready to go. Luis ran over and gave her a big hug. Then Mike went over and opened the back door, and Luis climbed in. The moving van was already sitting in the driveway at home with all their stuff in it. All that was left now were the handshakes and the farewells. They were going to miss this place.

They stopped at a fast-food place to pick up a burger for the road, and by then Mike's mind was made up. Then he found another one, an old silver one he'd used for the middle-school girls' games last year.

"Now you coach one team and I'll coach the other," he told Luis, "and you get to be ref."

They went outside to the front yard and marked a goal with some rocks and played for an hour. Mike tried to make every call exactly right.

So what did Mike do? I asked him this recently, and I was expecting the answer that most people expected when they heard about the call. He's a dad, after all. It's his kid's last game, and there's a shot at the state semifinals on the line.

He blew the whistle, he said, because he had no choice. You have to call what you see, he said. There's no other way to do it and stay a referee. The rules are the rules. The parents around him had said as much. Luis had come over to him and said the same thing: You have to call it, Dad, even if it's me.

He blew the whistle for a direct free kick to the Rangers, which put the ball just outside the Hawks' penalty box but not so far that they could quickly clear it. One of the kids on the Rangers dribbled it in, cut inside, and fired from about sixteen yards. The shot banged off the left post and went in.

Mike's family sat in shocked silence. His wife cried. His daughter, who also played on the team, came over to give her brother a hug but then burst into tears and ran off the field. They lost 2–1, but it didn't matter. Mike had made the right call.

What makes a referee? This question has been on my mind lately, because of a study that came out this spring from researchers in Canada. The paper, which was published in the European Journal of Social Psychology, was titled, bluntly, Does Being a Fan Make a Referee Biased? The answer was yes, though not necessarily in the way you might expect.

The study won't surprise anybody who's spent any time around youth sports and has seen parents who used to scream themselves hoarse from the sidelines suddenlyiken up a whistle and think they're God. The mere act of becoming a referee seems to bring with it a strong identification with a team. The Canadian researchers found that sport officials who were also fans of a particular league or team — even casually — tended to give more favorable calls to the group they liked once they blew the first whistle.

Mike didn't make Luis take a kick. They didn't have to. Mike had made his call, and if anybody had a question it was lost in the celebration of the division title and the win–13 to 10 on penalties. The Hawks would go on to the state tournament.

He had ruined his son's life, probably, or certainly complicated it, putting him in that position when the whole team wanted only to win. But there was no other choice. Everybody knew that. Mike knew it. And when he brought Luis over to the Rangers to shake hands after the game, nobody looked at him like he was a villain. They took the family's address so they could send Luis a tournament T-shirt.

The next day Mike learned from an official with the California Ovations soccer organization that he was disqualified from officiating for two years. His manual was clear: "A player who handles the ball deliberately . . . even if the ball strikes the hand on its way to the goal. . .incurs a direct free kick." While Mike respected the rule, he believed the offense needed to be consistent with the seriousness of the violation.

He also knew that, as an adult in a small community and the father of a player, the better call was letting the kids play. Some would say he'd been too harsh; some would say he hadn't been harsh enough.

Either way, he'd saved the game, though he'd lost the job he'd taken such pride in. That night he sat at the kitchen table in their house in Visalia and tried to explain to his son what he'd done. "Was the call right?" he asked.

"Yeah," Luis said.

"I had to make the call," Mike said.

"I know. You make all the right calls."

He hugged his son. Mike Delgado had never been prouder of him, or more sorry for him, or less sure of what he'd done.

If they lost on appeals, he'd be stripped of his certification. Tulare County would never hire him again. And Phoenix didn't have a youth soccer association as good as this one.

But the handball rule was the handball rule.

There are referees, and there are referees' sons. I am the latter. Football, netball, soccer, badminton: if anybody at the school volunteered to run a game, there was a solid chance my dad was the one who agreed to go. On any given weekend, a home game might be added to a day off from work, work added to a day off from school, and my brother and I became accustomed to the extra drive and the slightly longer day in the car. It wasn't easy for us, children, to recognize that the benefits for the schools were huge: sometimes for months they would rely on my dad for games, before they could find another adult to officiate, or before enough parent helpers were available. Mostly we just knew that no sport reached its full potential without an adult referee.

The last five minutes of a football game are the hardest. I sat in countless dugouts, overhearing coached and captained debates about how to calculate risk, the best move by a referee's own rules, the likely response. I sat on the track at the cricket oval, listening to friends say, that he might give it, or that he definitely wouldn't give it, until I, too, wondered what would be enough. Tennis was always more fraught—my dad umpired on the one line he could see both the whole court and the ball from, and by the end of the sixth 40–40 deuce he would gesture for the ballperson to have extra hawk-eyes getting ready. And even the badminton: the rule book, in a previous life, my dad used to say, had clearly been handed out at the same drawer as the rule books for the other Olympic sports.

Every year, the schools introduced a new rule about which games Dad couldn't referee, about how many games he could do in a week, how many he could do in a row. But on any given weekend, at any given school, it was still most likely him. I can't remember his rules.

The coach of the losing team nodded. "That was a handball, referee. We didn't get the win, but it's OK. Maybe the referee made a bad call, but he did it well." She winked at the referee. "And tomorrow they're going to get a nice referee appreciation dinner."

Its Victorian founders believed that ruffians were created by the conditions of industrialization. They believed that the problems of their era—massive poverty, horrific working conditions, political disfranchisement, disease—could be cured but not completely eradicated.
